newsitem.title: FRANCE: French Communists probe aims to silence party-Hue.
newsitem.headline: French Communists probe aims to silence party-Hue.

text.p: French Communist chief Robert Hue charged on Tuesday that a corruption probe targeting party leaders including himself was intended to silence the Communists at a time when they were gaining in strength.

"They (Authorities) are trying to extinguish the voice of a political party and a newspaper which have been denouncing the rule of money in French society...This is absolutely intolerable," Hue told radio France-Info.

The party newspaper L'Humanite confirmed on Tuesday that Hue, his predecessor Georges Marchais, party treasurer Pierre Sotura and L'Humanite editor Richard Beninger had been formally placed under investigation for alleged influence peddling.
The four men were informed of the judicial action last week but the information became public only late on Monday.
France has been rocked by a string of political funding scandals in recent years, touching all of the mainstream parties. But none has reached so high into a party's leadership.
Justice sources said the probe led by Paris magistrate Laurence Vichnievsky was part of an investigation into illicit funding of the Communist Party.

They said it centred on suspected bribes or kickbacks paid to the party by the French utilities giant Compagnie Generale des Eaux (CGE) in 1992-1994 in connection with the award of water contracts in some 70 mainly leftist towns.
L'Humanite said the probe was looking at commercial activities linked to the party's annual "Fete de l'Humanite" festival.
French media reported that the four men had been named in their function as party leaders rather than because they themselves were suspected of illegal acts.
The step of formally opening an investigation could lead to a trial but does not imply guilt.
Magistrate Vichnievsky had searched Communist Party headquarters in June as part of a probe of nearly 13 million francs ($2.5 million) in suspicious billing by the CGE.

In May, four former managers of the private consulting firm Sicopar, a subsidiary of the Gifco group, were placed under investigation in connection with the case on suspicion of acting as middlemen. Gifco was dissolved in 1994.
Hue denied any wrongdoing or irregularities and said party finances were totally open to public scrutiny.
"It is clear that they want to damage the Communist Party at a time it is forcefully denouncing the role of money in the nation and at a time when it is getting results," he said.
"These judicial steps appear to be a deliberate attack on the French Communist Party and its press," the party said in a statement.
